extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policymakers studying NIH grant funding and racial/ethnic disparities (NIH administrators, social scientists, grant applicants)
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of NIH R01 award disparities
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study of how applicants' self-identified race/ethnicity and related applicant-, training-, publication-, and employer-level factors are associated with the probability of receiving an NIH R01 investigator-initiated research award (FY2000–2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority score strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals with strong priority scores were equally likely to be funded regardless of race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that the NIH peer-review priority score is a strong predictor of funding and that when priority scores are strong, racial differences in funding probability disappear; suggests assessing applications by priority score can mask upstream disparities in scoring or application quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant self-identified race/ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Asians are 4 percentage points and black or African-American applicants are 13 percentage points less likely to receive NIH investigator-initiated research funding compared with whites; after controlling for covariates, black applicants remain 10 percentage points less likely than whites to be awarded NIH research funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Race/ethnicity is treated as an independent predictor of award probability, with statistically significant disparities (figures report P-values: ‡ P < .001; ** P < .01; * P < .05). Findings point to potential policy intervention points to address these disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant educational background
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant's educational background is included as a control variable in the analysis of award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational background (degree type, institution, etc.) is considered a substantive factor explaining differences in award likelihood and should be measured and adjusted for when assessing racial/ethnic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country of origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Country of origin of the applicant is used as a covariate in modeling award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes U.S.-born from foreign-born applicants; controlling for country of origin helps separate effects of race/ethnicity from immigration-related differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training / prior NIH F or T training program participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous NIH F or T training program participation is examined; figures compare within-race applications and applicants with or without such training and the differential effect compared with white participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation in NIH training programs is treated as a measurable input that can alter award probability; analyses stratify or control for training to assess its mediating/moderating role on race effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previous research awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior research awards held by the applicant are included as a control in the analysis of R01 award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior funding history is an indicator of applicant track record and institutional access; it is used to account for cumulative advantage when estimating race/ethnicity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication record
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant publication record (from Thomson Reuters Web of Science and other sources) is included as a covariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication quantity/quality is operationalized and controlled for to assess whether differences in scholarly output explain funding disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer characteristics / institutional affiliation and NIH funding rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer characteristics and institutional affiliation are accounted for; effects of affiliation and previous research on R01 award probability are shown (institutions ranked by NIH funding received, e.g., 1–30 and 31–100).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional prestige/NIH funding level is a substantive predictor; analyses demonstrate how institutional ranking and employer features alter award probabilities and interact with applicant race/ethnicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of linked administrative and bibliometric data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The study uses data from NIH IMPAC II grant database, Thomson Reuters Web of Science, AAMC Faculty Roster, and other sources to model award probability (N = 83,188 for FY2000–2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining administrative grant records with bibliometric and roster data provides comprehensive covariates for modeling; researchers should document data provenance and linkage methods to support validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling and significance testing of award probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood functions and statistical models (models, statistical significance thresholds) are used to estimate the probability of R01 award and to test race/ethnicity effects (figures report P < .05, P < .01, P < .001 thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ appropriate multivariate models with controls for confounders; report sample sizes, effect sizes (percentage-point differences), and P-values; stratified analyses (e.g., within-race comparisons, by training participation, by institutional rank) help elucidate mechanisms.
